extracted.intended_audience: owners/operators of combustion turbine EGUs, environmental regulators, state air agencies, industry stakeholders, and environmental/policy counsel
extracted.subtask_description: EPA determinations of the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) and related standards of performance for newly constructed and reconstructed stationary combustion turbine electric generating units, separated by low-, intermediate-, and base-load subcategories. Includes technical, cost, demonstration, operational, and environmental-impact considerations used to select or reject candidate BSERs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcategory definitions (low, intermediate, base load)
rubrics_metrics.description: Low load: combustion turbines selling 20 percent or less of potential electric output; Intermediate load: selling >20 percent and <=40 percent; Base load: selling >40 percent of potential electric output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These thresholds (based on percent of potential electric output sold) determine which BSER and standard of performance apply to a given combustion turbine. The low-load category is narrower than the 2015 NSPS non-base load definition (EPA lowered the electric sales threshold). Calculations of net electric sales use rolling averages (see background description in the 2015 NSPS).

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER for Low Load Subcategory: use of lower-emitting fuels
rubrics_metrics.description: The BSER for the low load (peaking) subcategory is the use of lower-emitting fuels (EPA proposed and is finalizing fuels with emissions rate <160 lb CO2/MMBtu as meeting BSER requirements for low load).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: variability of non-base load operation makes output-based standards impracticable; natural gas (with small allowance for Nos. 1 and 2 distillate oils) is technically feasible, widely used, and low cost; minimal additional energy or non-air impacts. EPA also references the 2015 NSPS where a heat-input based standard and fuels-based BSER were used (previously 120 lb CO2/MMBtu).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform fuels criteria and inclusion of low-GHG hydrogen
rubrics_metrics.description: Fuels meeting the fuels criterion include natural gas, Nos. 1 and 2 fuel oils, and EPA is finalizing the inclusion of hydrogen (regardless of production pathway) on the list of fuels meeting the uniform fuels criteria in 40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTTa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including hydrogen simplifies recordkeeping and reporting for low load turbines electing to burn hydrogen. The Agency treats these fuels as qualifying for the clean-fuels BSER for low-load units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficient design and operation do not qualify as BSER for low load
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA did not propose that efficient design and operation qualify as the BSER for the low load subcategory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: emissions of low-load turbines are highly dependent on operational patterns (starts/stops, part-load operation) rather than design efficiency measured at steady-state full load; insufficient information to determine emissions reductions and cost-effectiveness of a design-based BSER for this subcategory.

rubrics_metrics.name: CCS and hydrogen co-firing not BSER for low load
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA did not propose CCS or hydrogen co-firing as the BSER (or component) for low load combustion turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale for CCS: post-combustion amine-based CCS requires cooled exhaust (HRSG), which simple cycle units lack, plus high costs for low-load units. Rationale for hydrogen co-firing: not all new turbines can co-fire high % hydrogen, infrastructure issues, and infrequent utilization of low-load units may make hydrogen co-firing not cost-effective for all low-load turbines. EPA may evaluate these technologies further in future rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER for Intermediate Load Subcategory: highly efficient simple cycle + best O&M practices
rubrics_metrics.description: For intermediate load combustion turbines, the BSER is the use of high-efficiency simple cycle turbine technology in combination with the best operating and maintenance (O&M) practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA determined that at higher capacity factors, emission rates are more consistent so an output-based (design/efficiency-based) BSER is appropriate. The determination rests on commercial availability and demonstrated use by multiple facilities. The EPA sets a standard of performance reflecting this BSER at 1,170 lb CO2/MWh-gross for intermediate load turbines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower-emitting fuels not BSER for intermediate load
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA did not propose and is not finalizing lower-emitting fuels as the BSER for intermediate load combustion turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: lower-emitting fuels would achieve few GHG reductions compared to adopting highly efficient generation at intermediate capacity factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highly efficient generation technologies and best operating/maintenance practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly efficient generation includes technology and practices for simple cycle and combined cycle turbines (e.g., increasing firing temperature, increasing pressure ratios, intercooling, inlet air cooling, proper maintenance of flow path components, efficient HRSG design for combined cycle including multi-pressure HRSGs, steam reheat, insulation, blowdown heat recovery). Best O&M includes minimizing steam leaks, minimizing air infiltration, cleaning/maintaining heat transfer surfaces, and routine maintenance to minimize fuel use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA describes technology options, tradeoffs (efficiency vs flexibility), and design constraints (exhaust temperature, steam turbine size affecting HRSG options). The agency considered but did not include some emerging technologies (pressure gain combustion, supercritical steam or sCO2 cycles, fuel preheating) as BSER because they were insufficiently evaluated in the proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately demonstrated criterion for BSER selection
rubrics_metrics.description: A technology is 'adequately demonstrated' if it has been demonstrated by multiple facilities for decades, the efficiency improvements are incremental and do not change operations/maintenance significantly, and the levels of efficiency have been achieved by many recently constructed turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA uses 'adequately demonstrated' as a statutory factor when deciding whether a technology can be the BSER; commercial availability and achievability of performance standards are key elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs criterion for BSER selection
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA assesses capital costs, fuel cost impacts, levelized cost of electricity (LCOE), and cost-effectiveness to determine whether costs of adopting a technology as BSER are reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: EPA estimates high-efficiency simple cycle turbines cost ~10% more capital but use ~8% less fuel; at certain capacity factors this yields lower LCOE; for base load, high-efficiency combined cycle EGUs are ~1.9% higher capital cost and ~2.6% lower fuel use, with fuel savings offsetting capital over 30 years at >=40% capacity factor. EPA notes uncertainty in estimates and that some high-efficiency technology is already in common use absent regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-air quality health and environmental impacts and energy requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluates whether adopting a BSER would have significant adverse non-air quality health or environmental impacts or significant adverse energy requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA concluded use of highly efficient generation reduces non-air quality impacts and energy requirements because improved efficiency lowers fuel use for same output and reduces other pollutants; designation of highly efficient generation as BSER is not expected to have significant nationwide impacts on electricity supply, prices, or sector structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of reductions in CO2 emissions (quantification requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA assesses and estimates the potential CO2 (and co-pollutant NOX) reductions associated with a BSER-based standard of performance using historical data on newly constructed turbines and projecting reductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA methodology examples: for intermediate load, EPA set 1,170 lb CO2/MWh-gross and estimated ~31,000 tons CO2/year reductions based on turbines built 2015–2022; for base load, EPA set 800 lb CO2/MWh-gross and estimated ~313,000 tons CO2/year (increasing with time). Estimation method: identify turbines with emissions above the standard, calculate reductions to the standard at average capacity factor, sum and annualize over study years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of development and implementation of technology
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considers whether selecting a given BSER would promote the development and broader implementation of improved control or generation technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA finds that standards reflecting the performance of highly efficient units can promote penetration of most efficient units throughout the industry, which is a supporting factor in BSER selection but not determinative alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steam injection and other emerging technologies considered but not included as BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considered steam injection (and other technologies like pressure gain combustion, supercritical steam/sCO2 HRSG, fuel preheating) as potential ways to reduce emissions but did not include them as BSER because they are not adequately demonstrated or sufficiently evaluated in the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steam injection may improve efficiency and output and reduce NOX and has characteristics between simple and combined cycle, but EPA found limited demonstration and commenters questioned adequacy of analysis. EPA may evaluate these further in future rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational characteristics affecting BSER applicability (startup times, minimum runtimes, starts per year, hours/start ratio)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational limits and characteristics (e.g., startup time differences between simple cycle and combined cycle, minimum run times, minimum downtime, limits on starts per year, maintenance cost impacts when hours/start ratio drops) affect whether certain technologies can serve the same grid role and thus qualify as BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifics cited: simple cycle hot start to full load 5–8 minutes (cold start 10 min); combined cycle hot start 30–90 min (cold start 120–250 min); minimum run times: aeroderivative simple cycle 1 minute, combined cycle 120 minutes; minimum downtime: 5 minutes and 60 minutes respectively; combined cycle EGUs limited in number of starts and incur extra maintenance if hours/start <25. These operational constraints inform EPA's conclusion that combined cycle designs may not substitute for simple cycle units in intermediate load roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER for Base Load Subcategory — First Component: high-efficiency combined cycle + best O&M
rubrics_metrics.description: For base load combustion turbines, the first component of the BSER is the use of high-efficiency combined cycle technology in combination with best operating and maintenance practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA finds highly efficient combined cycle designs adequately demonstrated and commercially available. EPA proposes less stringent standards for smaller base load turbines (base load ratings <2,000 MMBtu/h) due to HRSG efficiency differences. The standard of performance reflecting this BSER is 800 lb CO2/MWh-gross for base load turbines. EPA estimates annual CO2 reductions and finds costs reasonable because fuel savings over a 30-year life offset slightly higher capital costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from ACE Rule 'heat rate improvements' (rebound effect consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA distinguishes 'highly efficient generation' as BSER for new/reconstructed turbines from the 'heat rate improvements' (HRI) BSER it set for existing coal-fired EGUs in the ACE Rule, noting HRIs can cause a 'rebound effect' (increased dispatch/hours) that may increase overall CO2 emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's technical judgment is that including highly efficient generation for new/reconstructed turbines does not present the same rebound-risk concerns because such new units are more likely to displace coal or less efficient turbines rather than increase total dispatch in a way that raises emissions or displace renewables.
